faq.q: What is inside a wireless charging pad?
faq.a: A flat coil of copper wire and a circuit that drives a rapidly changing current through it, more than a hundred thousand times a second for the common Qi standard. That makes a changing magnetic field above the pad.
asks: How does a charging pad make a field?

faq.q: How does energy get through the air?
faq.a: By magnetism. The changing magnetic field from the pad's coil reaches through a few millimetres of air and plastic into the phone, with no wires needed.

faq.q: How does the phone turn the field back into electricity?
faq.a: A matching coil inside the phone sits in the changing field, which induces an alternating current in it, just as in a transformer. A circuit then turns it into steady direct current.
asks: What is the coil in my phone for?

faq.q: Why does wireless charging get warm?
faq.a: Some energy is lost as heat in the coils and circuits, especially if the phone is not lined up well, so wireless charging is a little less efficient than a cable.
asks: Is wireless charging slower than a cable?

faq.q: Why does my phone have to be in the right spot on the pad?
faq.a: The two coils must be close and lined up for the field to pass through the phone's coil. Off-centre, less of the field reaches it, so charging slows or stops. Some phones use magnets to snap into place.
asks: Why does my phone stop charging when it slides?

facts: The common Qi wireless charging standard works across only a few millimetres between the coils.
Electric toothbrushes have used inductive charging for decades, sealed away from water.
